trivia_fact: Systemd is one of the most controversial projects in Linux history. When Debian voted to adopt it in 2014, the debate was so heated it led to the "Debian Civil War," a fork (Devuan), and multiple developers leaving the project. The debate centered on systemd violating the Unix philosophy of "do one thing well."

Lennart Poettering created systemd at Red Hat in 2010, along with Kay Sievers. Poettering had previously created PulseAudio (also controversial) and Avahi. He argued that SysV init's sequential shell script startup was fundamentally broken for modern systems with parallelism and dynamic hardware.

Systemd runs as PID 1, replacing SysV init. PID 1 has unique kernel properties: it cannot be killed by signals it doesn't handle, and it inherits all orphaned processes. Systemd leverages this by managing the entire process lifecycle — spawning, monitoring, and restarting services automatically.

Systemd has absorbed functionality previously handled by separate tools: init, cron (systemd timers), syslog (journald), network config (networkd), DNS resolution (resolved), login management (logind), device management (udevd), and even a boot loader (systemd-boot). Critics call it "the systemd OS."

The running joke that "systemd is an operating system" became so widespread that it has its own Know Your Meme-style documentation. The humor stems from systemd steadily absorbing functionality: "Give it time and systemd will replace the kernel too." Poettering has called such criticism "FUD."

Systemd's socket activation — where systemd listens on a socket and starts the service on first connection — is actually an old idea. inetd (1983) did the same thing for network services. Systemd generalized it to any socket type (Unix, FIFO, D-Bus) and made it a core service management pattern.

Systemd places every service in its own cgroup, solving a fundamental problem of SysV init: reliably tracking all processes belonging to a service. With cgroups, you can't escape systemd's oversight by double-forking — a technique that made SysV init lose track of daemon processes.

SysV init (1983) used numbered shell scripts (S01, S02...) run sequentially at boot. The replacement debate produced Upstart (Ubuntu, 2006), OpenRC (Gentoo), runit, and systemd. Systemd won most distros by 2015 through parallelized boot, dependency-based ordering, and aggressive corporate backing from Red Hat.

Journald stores logs in a binary format instead of plain text files, which infuriated Unix traditionalists who relied on grep/awk/sed to analyze /var/log/syslog. Proponents argue binary logs enable structured querying (journalctl), built-in rotation, and tamper-evident sealing that text logs cannot provide.

SysV init started services sequentially: service A, then B, then C. Systemd starts them in parallel based on dependency graphs, reducing boot times dramatically. It can even start a service before its dependencies are fully ready (via socket activation), then block only if the service actually needs the dependency.

Systemd unit files use a declarative INI-style format instead of imperative shell scripts. A service definition states what should happen (ExecStart, Restart, Dependencies) rather than how. This makes units easier to parse, analyze, and generate — but harder to debug when they don't work as expected.

Devuan is a Debian fork created in 2014 specifically to provide a systemd-free distribution. The "Veteran Unix Admins" who started it argued that hard-coupling to systemd violated user choice. Devuan supports multiple init systems (sysvinit, OpenRC, runit) and maintains its own package repository with systemd dependencies removed.
